concise

/kun-SYSE/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Concise means brief and direct in expression — saying everything that needs saying in the fewest words that will do it.

Editors loved her concise match reports: ninety minutes of soccer delivered in six tight sentences.

Example

At Gettysburg, the featured orator Edward Everett spoke for two hours; Lincoln followed with 272 words. Everett wrote to him the next day that the president had come nearer the occasion's central idea in two minutes than he himself had in two hours — the finest tribute one speaker ever paid a concise one.

Two minutes, every word pulling its weight, nothing that mattered left unsaid — expression that brief and that direct is exactly what concise means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

succinct: Succinct means compactly and neatly complete — nearly a twin of concise. Succinct leans toward praise for the elegance of the compression; concise is the plainer, matter-of-fact word for saying it in few words.

terse: Terse means stripped so bare it can read as cold or curt — terse brevity has an edge to it. Concise brevity stays civil: nothing extra, but nothing chilly either.

pithy: Pithy means brief and loaded — a pithy line carries wit or wisdom concentrated into a phrase. Concise promises only economy; a grocery list can be concise, but it takes a proverb to be pithy.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

verbose: using far more words than the message needs

rambling: wandering from point to point with no direction home

Where it sits · how hard the wording is pared down

economical → concise → curt

economical vs. concise: Economical wording is milder than concise: it trims obvious excess but keeps its comfortable phrases, while concise writing pares everything down to the words that earn their place.

curt vs. concise: Curt goes further than concise: concise trims a message to its essentials and stays polite, while a curt reply is cut so short it borders on rude.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-: thoroughly (Latin, used here as an intensifier)

Root — -cise: to cut (Latin caedere; cut-stem -cis-)

Put it together: Latin concidere — con- (here meaning 'thoroughly') plus caedere ('to cut') — meant 'to cut up, to cut down.' Concise writing is writing that has been cut: every spare word trimmed away until only the working ones remain. The same cutting root leaves its mark in scissors and incision.

Use the root in a new word: incisive: One incisive question from the back row changed the direction of the entire board meeting.

Root Check

Word Choice

approving — praise for discipline in writing

Concise is almost always a compliment: it certifies that every word earns its place. It measures length against need — which is why it differs from this unit's lucid, a claim about clarity rather than brevity: a concise note can still confuse, and a lucid lecture can fill an afternoon. Push brevity past politeness and you land on terse or curt; keep the essentials and you stay concise. Teachers asking for 'a concise answer' are asking you to cut, not to omit.
